alt: イセエビ, ホンエビ, 具足海老, イソエビ, 志摩海老, 鎌倉海老
intro: Iseebi is the spiny lobster of the Japanese Pacific coast. Its name is attributed to Ise: the Edo-period work Yamato Honzo is quoted as saying that many of these shrimp came from Ise, hence the name. Several place-linked trade names exist, and fishing seasons and legal size limits differ by prefecture, so the origin on the label matters more than any single national grade.

seasons.t: Sources say the eating season is generally autumn to winter as seawater cools, with differences by locality.
Closed seasons differ by prefecture: Mie 1 May-30 Sep; Chiba 1 Jun-31 Jul; Wakayama and Shizuoka 1 May-15 Sep (as reported by the sources).

names.t: Name used for iseebi from the Shima area of Mie.
Name for iseebi taken off Kamakura.
Brand-style name for Soto-Boso (outer Boso coast) lobster.

flavor: The consulted sources describe season rather than flavor in detail; the autumn-to-winter season is the one they treat as best for eating.
use: Sold for sashimi and whole-body grilled dishes (sugata-yaki) according to the tourism and gift-shop sources consulted.
craft: Regulation is the main handling fact in the sources: in Mie, lobsters with a carapace (head to body) of 4.2 cm or less must be released. Closed seasons run roughly May to September but differ by prefecture. For recreational fishing, a 20 cm total-length minimum is cited for southern Boso (Chiba), the Miura Peninsula (Kanagawa) and Oarai (Ibaraki); the sources note large specimens reach about 30 cm. Other names listed by the sources: honebi (ホンエビ), gusoku-ebi (具足海老, armor shrimp) and iso-ebi. The sources consulted did not give market size grades or kill/ageing technique, so none are stated here.
src: Gourmet Caree - origin of the name Iseebi

alt: クルマエビ, 活車海老
intro: Kuruma-ebi is traded live, and its size is called by a small ladder of growth-stage names (saimaki, maki, kuruma, o-kuruma). Today around 90 percent of the supply is said to be farmed. Sources disagree on the best season, which is a real trade issue.

seasons.t: One fish-information site gives 11 Feb as the season: in winter dormancy glycine rises and sweetness increases. Farmed prawns from Kume are shipped Nov-end Mar.
A gift-shop source puts wild prawns at Jun-Aug and another at Jun-Sep. The sources therefore split between a summer wild season and a winter season.

systems.label: Okinawa / Kagoshima / Kumamoto (main farming zone cited)

names.t: Smallest stage.
Small.

names.s: larger than maki; up to 25 cm or more
names.t: Standard size.
Not given a cm figure in the sources.

flavor: Sweetness is attributed to glycine accumulation in cold-season dormancy by one source; the sources gave no other sensory description.
use: Sold as live farmed prawns by weight per head for tempura, sushi and grilling (use is implied by the trade pages rather than described in detail).
craft: Piece weight is the practical grade: a Toyosu dealer lists live farmed prawns at 20-30 g per piece, with larger lots around 40 g. A Kume Island producer gives about 25 g as its standard size and ships from November to the end of March. One dealer says Okinawa, Kagoshima and Kumamoto hold about 80 percent of national farmed output. Stage names saimaki/maki/kuruma/o-kuruma are described by Toyosu sources; the Okinawa cm figures are 10 cm or less, about 15 cm, and larger, with a maximum over 25 cm. Sources disagree on season (summer vs winter), so confirm with the supplier whether the lot is wild or farmed.

alt: トヤマエビ, 富山蝦
intro: The botan-ebi sold on most markets today is mostly Toyama-ebi, according to the sources. The true botan-ebi is said to be caught only on the Pacific side of Honshu. Some sources also warn that much of what is sold in supermarkets as botan-ebi is imported spot shrimp.

seasons.t: One source gives Sep-May as the season.

systems.label: Hokkaido (Toyama-ebi documented by the prefectural fisheries office)

names.t: What is usually sold as botan-ebi.

flavor: The consulted sources compare botan-ebi with amaebi but give no usable flavor description here.
use: Sold raw as sushi and sashimi shrimp.
craft: Size is given as 13-20 cm. The true botan-ebi is reported as only caught on the Pacific side of Honshu; the botan-ebi on the market is mostly Toyama-ebi, and one source says many supermarket 'botan-ebi' are imported spot shrimp. When specifying, ask the supplier for the species, not only the trade name. The sources contained no grade table or handling steps.

intro: Amaebi is the trade name of the shrimp whose standard Japanese name is hokkoku-akaebi. It occurs from the Sea of Japan to Hokkaido, Alaska and the west coast of Canada. It is a raw sushi and sashimi shrimp.

seasons.t: Season is given as September to February.

names.t: Standard name; sold as amaebi.

flavor: Name and trade use imply sweetness; the sources consulted did not give a detailed sensory description.
craft: Size is about 10 cm. In the consulted sources, amaebi is distinguished from botan-ebi (Toyama-ebi, larger at 13-20 cm). The sources gave no grading or handling technique.

alt: シラエビ, シロエビ
intro: In Toyama the shrimp is called shiro-ebi, but its standard Japanese name is shira-ebi. It lives in deep water in Toyama Bay, Sagami Bay and Suruga Bay. It is a different shrimp from sakura-ebi, though the two look similar.

names.t: Standard name is shira-ebi.

flavor: No detailed flavor description was in the consulted result.
craft: Sources describe it as larger and whiter than sakura-ebi, which helps tell the two apart. Months are all marked 1 only as a placeholder: the search results gave no season, so none is asserted.

alt: サクラエビ, 由比の桜えび
intro: In Japan sakura-ebi is caught commercially only in Suruga Bay, Shizuoka. There are two fishing seasons, spring and autumn, with a closed summer. It is a small shrimp, 3-5 cm depending on the source.

seasons.t: Spring fishing from late March to early June.
Autumn fishing from late October to late December.

names.s: 3-4 cm or 4-5 cm depending on source
names.t: Sources disagree on body length.
Local brand name used by the Yui fishery site.

flavor: The consulted summaries gave no flavor detail.
use: Eaten fresh, dried, or fried; the sources consulted did not give specific cooking uses.
craft: Closed in summer. Lengths in the sources: 3-4 cm in some, 4-5 cm in others. Do not confuse with shiro-ebi (shira-ebi), which is a taxonomically different and larger, whiter shrimp.

intro: Hokkaido kegani is fished in a relay of local seasons, so it is available most of the year even though some sources call winter the true season. The season depends on the fishing ground, not just the calendar.

seasons.t: Okhotsk coast season March to June.
Funka Bay (Uchiura) July to August.
Off Nemuro September to December.
Off Hidaka December to February.

names.t: Season depends on fishing ground (see seasons).

flavor: The rich crab miso (kani-miso) is the feature emphasized.
use: Boiled whole; the sources consulted gave no specific cooking method for kegani.
craft: Sources disagree: some call winter the shun, while others stress the relay of seasons that keeps it on sale through the year. When buying, ask which fishing ground the crab came from; that fixes the season.

intro: Hanasaki-gani is landed only at Kushiro and Nemuro in Hokkaido. Despite the name, it belongs taxonomically to the hermit crab group, not the true crabs. It is called a rare, limited-catch crab.

seasons.t: Kushiro fishing season March to July.
Nemuro fishing season July to September.

names.t: Called a rare crab because of the narrow range and catch limits.

flavor: No flavor description was in the consulted result beyond its prized status.
craft: One source for raw crab: put the crab in heavily salted water shell-side down, boil 15-20 minutes, then shock in ice water. Common eating season is summer to early autumn.

latin: Magallana gigas (Crassostrea gigas); rock oyster Magallana nippona
alt: マガキ, 岩牡蠣, 岩ガキ
intro: Oysters are sold under production-area names such as Hiroshima and Akkeshi, and by two seasons: the winter Pacific oyster and the summer rock oyster. Raw sale in Japan is governed by food-standard rules on sea-area and purification.

seasons.t: Hiroshima harvest runs Oct-Apr, and Dec-Feb is the peak. Akkeshi is also described as best Dec-Feb.
Rock oyster, summer, Jun-Aug in most sources; eaten mainly raw.

names.t: Famous for shucked meat; about 20,000 t of shucked oysters a year are mentioned; many are for cooking.
Water is cold enough that raw oysters are said to be possible all year.

flavor: Sources do not give detailed sensory descriptions here.
use: Raw (must be sold as 'for raw eating'), or cooked.
craft: Raw-sale rules in the consulted source: oysters harvested in waters at 70 or lower E. coli group MPN per 100 mL qualify; others need purification in UV-sterilized seawater, which causes slight loss of body. Storage for raw oysters is 10 C or below. National production is cited as 158,789 t (Reiwa 3), with Hiroshima about 60 percent. Sources vary on the season (Oct-Mar, Dec-Apr). Matsushima and Iwagaki production areas were not documented in the results, so no claim is made.

alt: ホタテ, ホタテガイ, ベビーホタテ, 半成貝
intro: Hotate is farmed in Hokkaido and Aomori. The trade distinguishes baby scallops (half-grown, hansei-gai) from full-grown scallops, and farming method (hanging vs ground-seeded) changes texture. There are two seasonal peaks.

seasons.t: Large adductor muscle in May-Aug.

seasons.j: 卵・白子とベビーの旬
seasons.t: Roe, milt and baby scallop in Dec-Mar.

names.t: Less sand; body tends to be soft.
Thick, elastic adductor.

names.s: about 6 cm or 7-8 cm by seller
names.t: One-year-old half-grown shell; sellers differ on size.

flavor: Baby scallops are described as giving good stock (dashi).
use: Whole live baby scallops for steaming and grilling; adductor for raw use (the sources are sales pages).
craft: The Aomori 2025 spring survey found 2024-year half-grown shells averaged 6.1 cm, 1.3 cm below normal and the worst on record, so supply and size can vary by year. Sources say Okhotsk season varies by culture method; hanging is 3-4 and ground-seeding 8-9.

Daily Tohoku - Mutsu Bay scallop growth

latin: Haliotis discus discus (kuro), H. gigantea (madaka), H. madaka, H. discus hannai (ezo)
alt: アワビ, クロアワビ, メガイアワビ, マダカアワビ, エゾアワビ
intro: Japan trades four abalone: kuro-awabi, megai-awabi, madaka-awabi and ezo-awabi. They differ in size, shell shape, flesh texture and season, so naming the species matters when buying.

seasons.t: Kuro, megai and madaka are mostly said to be in season in summer; one source gives madaka summer-autumn and another megai winter-spring.
Ezo-awabi is northern and comes in later, Nov-Jan.

systems.label: Minami-Boso, Chiba (reference source on the abalone fishery)

names.t: Lives shallowest of the four, fast-moving.
Soft flesh, suited to cooking.
Biggest species.
Later season than the others.

flavor: Texture distinction only: megai is described as soft and suited to heat.
use: Raw and cooked; megai for cooked dishes.
craft: Spawning is autumn to early winter for kuro, madaka and megai, and summer to early autumn for ezo; many areas close fishing in late autumn, with dates set by local fishery rules. Sources conflict on megai and madaka seasons. Closed periods and minimum sizes were not in the results.

alt: ハマグリ, チョウセンハマグリ, ジハマグリ, 地ハマグリ
intro: Most hamaguri on the market is imported shina-hamaguri from China. The native hamaguri survives only in the Seto Inland Sea and western Kyushu coast, and Kuwana in Mie is the famous source. The 'ji-hamaguri' from Kujukuri and Kashima-nada is chosen-hamaguri.

seasons.t: Before spawning, April to July.
Kashima-nada February to mid-May; Kujukuri May-June.

names.t: Native; Akasuka port in Kuwana is cited; shell pattern shaped like 'ha' is preferred.

names.j: チョウセンハマグリ（地ハマグリ）
names.t: Domestic wild clam of the Kujukuri and Kashima-nada beaches.

flavor: No flavor detail in the consulted summaries.
use: Yaki-hamaguri and clear soup are the typical uses the sources suggest.
craft: Domestic hamaguri is said to be only about 10 percent of what circulates. Check species on the label: shina-hamaguri (imported), hamaguri (native), chosen-hamaguri. Season figures differ by source and area.

alt: ナマコ, 青ナマコ, 赤ナマコ, 黒ナマコ
intro: Aka-namako, ao-namako and kuro-namako are color types of the same species. The sources say they are classified as one species, though habitat differs, and regional preference differs: Kansai prefers crunchy aka, Kanto the softer ao.

seasons.t: Winter is the season.

names.t: Preferred for firm bite.
Softer; strong Kanto demand.

use: Raw slices, vinegared; black type is for dried product.
craft: Prep in the sources: wash the surface, cut open the belly (the side with fine bumps), cut off mouth and anus ends, rub with coarse salt to remove slime. Another method splits into back and belly and scrapes the organs. Kuro-namako is mainly dried for China and ranked highest in price (kuro, then aka, then ao).
src: Nagasaki Uo - aka and ao namako

alt: ホヤ, マボヤ, 真ホヤ
intro: Hoya from Miyagi is the standard maboya. Miyagi is described as the birthplace of hoya farming, with culture in the bays north of the Oshika Peninsula.

seasons.t: Miyagi landings May-Aug, best early July to the Obon holiday.

names.t: Standard Miyagi hoya.

flavor: Not described in the consulted summaries.
use: Eaten raw and in Tohoku cuisine (sources are general).
craft: Prep: cut off both siphons (intake and exhaust), open the shell, take out the body and remove the red-edged part, waste, the black liver and the gills. The shell can be used as a serving vessel. Aka-boya was not covered.

en: Sea urchin (bafun uni and murasaki uni)
alt: エゾバフンウニ, キタムラサキウニ, バフンウニ, ムラサキウニ
intro: Hokkaido uni is sold by species and by island or coast of origin. Bafun and murasaki have different fishing seasons, and sources disagree on exact windows.

seasons.t: Rishiri: kita-murasaki mid-June to mid-September, ezo-bafun mid-June to late August. Rebun ezo-bafun early June to mid-August, best until mid-July.
Rausu fishery January to end of June.

names.t: Rishiri and Rebun are rated highly; one source gives June-October.
June-August is main season per one source.

flavor: Spawning loosens the roe and lowers the taste.
use: Raw as sushi, uni-don; sold as salt-water pack.
craft: Roe quality falls after spawning begins. Sato Suisan sells Rishiri-Rebun ezo-bafun in a salt-water pack (shiomizu uni) and says harvesting opens in June. Alum treatment and shelf-life were not found.

alt: イクラ, バラ子, 筋子, すじこ
intro: Sujiko is the whole egg skein in its ovarian membrane. Ikura is the same roe with the membrane removed and separated into single grains. The two differ in grain size, salt level and handling.

systems.label: Nationwide trade names (placeholder pref: no regional ladder in sources)

names.t: Often immature eggs, grains slightly smaller; commonly salted, also soy-cured or kasu-zuke.

names.s: loose grains from ripe pre-spawning roe
names.t: Membrane removed.

flavor: No flavor description in the consulted results.
use: Sushi, rice bowls; sujiko as salted skein.
craft: Salt level cited from an instrument table: ikura 2.3 percent, sujiko 4.8 percent. Seasons and grades were not in the results.

alt: タラコ, 明太子, めんたいこ
intro: Both are pollock roe sacs. Tarako is the salt-cured roe. Mentaiko is cured and then seasoned with a liquid containing chili. Sources say the idea came from Korea and the name from the Korean word for pollock.

names.t: Unspiced versions are treated nearly as tarako.

flavor: Mentaiko adds chili heat; no further sensory detail in results.
use: The sources consulted did not state uses.
craft: No grading or process details in the results beyond the cure-versus-seasoned distinction. Months set to 1 as a placeholder.

intro: Kazunoko is salted herring roe. Its name is said to come from kado, the northern Tohoku name for herring. Sources also note that commercial kazunoko is often bleached with hydrogen peroxide.

names.t: Kado-no-ko led to kazunoko.
Salted ovary.

flavor: No sensory description in the results.
craft: The sources note common bleaching with hydrogen peroxide. Months are placeholders. Season, grades and desalting steps were not found.

latin: Engraulis japonicus (main species; other young fish are also sold as shirasu)
alt: シラス, 生しらす, 釜揚げしらす, しらす干し, ちりめんじゃこ
intro: Shirasu is sold as a ladder of states by water content: raw, kama-age, shirasu-boshi and chirimen-jako. Raw shirasu deteriorates quickly, so it is rarely available away from the landing area.

seasons.t: Best period given for raw shirasu, Jul-Sep; some say summer to autumn.
Many areas close January to mid-March to protect stock.

names.t: Deteriorates fast.

names.s: water about 77 percent (other source about 80 percent)
names.t: Salt-boiled and drained.
Sun- or machine-dried kama-age.
Drier still.
Fujisawa lists it as a local product.

craft: Shizuoka season is given as late March to mid-January in one article and as Jun-Sep in another; Hyogo as May-Nov. Water figures differ by source (kama-age about 77 or about 80 percent). Latin name given in the entry is not from the sources.
